In one fortnight of the course’s own data, 9.50 per cent of the 31,878 rule pairs are correlated at exactly one. In the next fortnight, 72.23 per cent are.

Lesson 73 ended on a covariance matrix with no inverse, and this is why. Cut the twenty-eight moves in half and count how many of lesson 71’s 31,878 rule pairs are correlated at exactly one. In the first fourteen, 9.50 per cent are. In the last fourteen, 72.23 per cent are, and 215 of the 253 rules produce a return series over that fortnight that is identical, number for number, to the slowest rule in the grid. The correlation this module has been spending is not a property of your rules. It is a property of the fortnight you measured it in, and the fortnight in which it is worst is the fortnight in which every rule is holding.

So count how often they are all in. Over the first fourteen moves, an average of 70.2 per cent of the 253 rules are holding a position on a given day, and on the quietest of those days it is 17.0 per cent. Over the last fourteen it is 97.4 per cent on the average day and never below 91.7 per cent. That is the whole story: in the second fortnight the grid is not a set of rules with different opinions, it is 253 copies of a long position with a few of them occasionally stepping out. Count the extreme of that and 215 of the 253 produce a return series over those fourteen moves that is identical, number for number, to the slowest rule in the grid.

The median pair in the last fourteen moves is correlated at one. Not close to one, at one: more than half of the 31,878 pairs in the grid produce the same fourteen numbers as each other. The middle row’s 8.93 per cent is lower than the first row’s 9.50 for a dull reason worth stating: agreeing on twenty-eight numbers is harder than agreeing on fourteen, so the longer window finds fewer exact ties even though it contains the fortnight in which almost everything tied. The full-window figure of 0.9472 that lesson 71 measured, and that lessons 72 and 73 spent, is an average of a fortnight in which a tenth of the grid was identical and a fortnight in which nearly three quarters of it was.

Before treating that as a finding, rule out the obvious objection: fourteen observations measure a correlation badly, so perhaps the two halves differ because any two halves would. That is testable. Take each pair’s twenty-eight-move correlation, hold it fixed as the truth, and simulate what two halves of fourteen draws each would show, ten times per pair from seed 20260907, which is 318,780 simulated splits. Under that null the median pair’s correlation moves by 0.0205 between halves and moves by more than 0.2 in 5.89 per cent of cases. What actually happens is that it moves by 0.0968, nearly five times as much, and moves by more than 0.2 in 27.2 per cent of pairs and by more than 0.4 in 13.7 per cent.

And the direction settles it. Sampling error is symmetric: half the pairs should rise and half should fall. In the measurement, 97.9 per cent of the 31,878 pairs rose. That is not noise, it is one thing happening to the whole grid at once.

Read the last column. The same four positions, sized identically, hand you a day on which everything goes against you 1.74 times more often when the correlation is measured on the second fortnight than on the first. Lesson 72’s finding was that heat is a maximum and correlation is the schedule; this table says the schedule is itself a function of when you looked.

The second column is worse than it looks. In the first fortnight the four rules are 1.48 independent bets, which is thin and is at least more than one. In the second they are 1.0599, which rounds to one bet in any language. You did not stop diversifying. The market stopped letting you.

And the third row is where lesson 73 stops working. Three of the six pairs are correlated at exactly one over those fourteen moves, so the covariance matrix has a determinant of zero, no inverse, and no minimum-variance weights of any kind. The optimiser does not return a bad allocation for that fortnight, it returns nothing at all. On the first fourteen it returns 0.308, 0.225, minus 0.731 and 1.197; on the full twenty-eight it returns 0.987, minus 0.438, minus 0.705 and 1.156; on the last fourteen the question has no answer.

So the practical rule is not about weights, it is about size. Price the book on the worst window you have measured rather than on the average of your windows, which on these four rules means planning for 1.06 bets and one bad day in 2.6 rather than 1.48 and one in 4.5.

That the comparison between the two windows is clean. It is not, and there is a known bias pointing the same way as the finding. The second fortnight is more volatile than the first, with the instrument’s own standard deviation 1.195 times higher, and measuring a correlation inside a more volatile stretch inflates it mechanically even when the underlying relationship has not moved at all. Apply the standard correction for that and the 0.9247 becomes 0.8972. Which still sits far above the first fortnight’s 0.5673, so the bias explains part of the move and not most of it, but a page that quoted 0.9247 without saying this would be overstating its own case.

That fourteen observations measure anything. On their own they measure very little, and a single pair split that way is worth nothing. What makes the movement credible is that the same split was applied to 31,878 pairs and compared against a simulation of what chance alone would do, which is a test the individual pair cannot pass and the grid can.
The all-against day, which arrives 1.74 times more often on the second fortnight than the first.
